body.heading: The doubling ladder
paragraphs: One yes-or-no question can distinguish between 2 possibilities. Two questions can handle 4, three questions 8. Each question doubles your reach: 10 questions cover 1,024 possibilities, and 20 questions cover 2 to the power 20 - 1,048,576. Over a million things, searchable with twenty careful questions. That is the entire engine of the parlour game Twenty Questions.

It is also the engine inside a great deal of computing. Searching a sorted list by repeatedly halving it - binary search - is the same trick wearing a lab coat. When a computer finds one name among a billion in a fraction of a second, it is playing Twenty Questions at electronic speed, needing only about 30 halvings.

body.heading: What makes a question good
paragraphs: A good question splits the remaining possibilities as evenly as possible. 'Is it alive?' divides the world usefully; 'Is it a toaster?' gambles everything on one item and usually wastes a turn. Early questions should be broad categories - animal, vegetable or mineral, in the classic opening - and later questions narrow in on the surviving branch.

You can feel the same strategy in number guessing. To find a secret number from 1 to 100, never guess randomly: guess 50, then halve the surviving range. Seven questions always suffice, because 2 to the power 7 is 128. Players who guess 'lucky' numbers instead are relying on the one strategy the maths cannot help.

body.heading: Try it yourself
paragraphs: Play the number game with a partner: they pick a number from 1 to 100, you halve relentlessly and count your questions - you should never need more than seven. Then play classic Twenty Questions and track how the possibility space shrinks after each answer.

Finally, try being the answerer with a deliberately tricky object, and notice which questions hurt most. The questions that split your category cleanly in half are the ones good players ask - and now you know their secret is arithmetic, not intuition.

takeaway: Halving is powerful: twenty well-chosen yes-or-no questions can search a million possibilities, because 2 to the power 20 is more than a million.
